opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest difference is that the visit starts to feel like a conversation again. For a long time, family doctors have essentially been doing two jobs at once: listening to the patient and typing up the encounter in real time. You've probably had the experience yourself, where your doctor is half-turned toward a screen while you're describing what's going on. An AI scribe takes a lot of that documentation burden off the table, so the physician can actually look at the patient, ask follow-up questions, and pick up on the things people don't always say outright.

I'd be careful about saying it automatically means longer appointments. What it changes is the *quality* of the time. The minutes in the room are spent more on the person and less on the keyboard. And then there's the time outside the room. A lot of family doctors have been finishing charts late at night, what people sometimes call "pajama time." Getting some of that back matters for burnout, and burnout matters for access. If doctors aren't leaving family practice, or can manage a slightly larger panel without running themselves into the ground, that ultimately means more patients have a family doctor at all.

That said, it's not magic. The physician still has to review and sign off on the note, and you have to think carefully about consent, privacy, and how the recordings and data are handled. But used well, I see it giving back something that's been eroding in primary care for years: undivided attention between a patient and their doctor.

r001.rationale: It says the physician can “actually look at the patient” instead of focusing on typing.

r002.rationale: It describes more time for conversation and follow-up questions, but does not say scribes free time for physical examinations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the difference shows up in two places, and only one of them is about minutes.

The first is the visit itself. Before scribes, a family doctor was splitting their attention between the patient and the screen, typing while listening, trying to capture enough that the note would be defensible later. When an ambient scribe is recording and drafting the note, the laptop can close. The doctor can actually look at the person in front of them. Patients notice that immediately, and physicians tell us it's the part of the job they went into medicine for. So even if the appointment is still fifteen minutes, more of those fifteen minutes are real conversation rather than data entry.

The second place is after hours, and I think this is where the bigger impact is. The so-called pajama time, where doctors finish charts at nine at night, is a major driver of burnout. In the evaluations we've seen in Alberta and elsewhere, physicians are reporting something on the order of an hour or more a day back from documentation. That doesn't always translate into longer appointments, but it does translate into doctors who stay in family practice, who take on a few more patients, or who simply aren't exhausted when they walk into the next room. In a province where a lot of people don't have a family doctor at all, keeping physicians in the system is arguably the most important time dividend.

I'd add a couple of cautions, because I don't think the technology sells itself. The notes still need to be reviewed, and a scribe that produces a plausible but wrong note is worse than no scribe. Privacy and consent have to be handled properly, especially with patients who may not be comfortable being recorded. And we need to study this with real outcome measures, not just satisfaction surveys. But if you ask me what I'm seeing on the ground, it's that the relationship in the room gets better, and the physician gets part of their life back. Those are both worth a lot.

r001.rationale: It says the doctor can close the laptop and “actually look at the person in front of them,” identifying increased visual attention during visits.

r002.rationale: It describes more conversation and less data entry, but does not say scribes free time for physical examinations.

astra-6.text: I think the biggest difference is that patients can have more of their doctor’s attention. If an AI scribe can take on the work of drafting the note, the doctor can spend less of the visit typing and more of it listening, making eye contact, and asking questions. That doesn’t necessarily mean the appointment gets longer, but it could make the time together feel less rushed and more focused on the patient. The doctor still needs to review the note, and patients need to understand and be comfortable with how the technology is being used.

r001.rationale: It says the doctor can spend less time typing and more time making eye contact with the patient.

r002.rationale: It mentions more time listening, making eye contact, and asking questions, but does not say AI scribes free time for physical examinations.
